transfer.scenario: Re-use your design for a utility company's assistant that can book engineer visits and apply bill credits after outages. What changes, and what stays?
rubric: router plus workflows for common intents|workflow first
credit tool capped and approved above a threshold|human approval
idempotency key per credit|one credit per outage per account
booking system is flaky: timeouts, retries, fallback|timeouts and retries|fallback
evaluate on real past conversations with repeated trials|repeated trials|real past conversations

brief: A parcel-delivery company handling 2 million deliveries a month wants an assistant in its app and website. It should answer 'where is my parcel', reschedule deliveries, update drop-off instructions, and issue goodwill credits when a parcel is late. Today 120 support staff do this by hand. The assistant must use the existing tracking API, a scheduling service that sometimes times out at peak, and a billing system. Last year a scripted bot issued duplicate credits during a billing outage, and finance has not forgotten. The company already runs on AWS.

clarifications.reveal: About 4,000 conversations a day. Roughly 70% are 'where is my parcel', 15% reschedules, 10% credit requests, 5% anything else.
Policy: one credit per parcel, only if tracking shows it late. Credits up to 10 dollars can be automatic; above that, a supervisor must approve.
Logged-in customers are identified by their account. Guests can track with a tracking number plus postcode, but only the account holder may reschedule, change instructions or get credits.
The scheduling service times out on about 2% of calls at peak. The billing API accepts an idempotency key and treats a repeated key as a duplicate, returning the original result.
Drop-off instructions are free text typed by customers and shown to drivers. Some contain long messages, links and odd text.

Tracking answers should come back in about 2 seconds, other actions within 6. Finance wants a cost per resolved conversation well below today's staff cost, and will set the target once it sees a pilot.
Support can export 5,000 past conversations with outcomes. Leadership's bar: zero wrong or duplicate credits, and at least the current resolution rate.

constraints: Only the account holder may reschedule, change instructions or receive a credit.
One credit per parcel, only when tracking shows it late; credits above 10 dollars need supervisor approval.
No duplicate credits, including during outages and retries.
Customer free text (instructions, messages) is untrusted.
Tracking answers in about 2 seconds; other actions within about 6 seconds.
A cost per resolved conversation that finance can track.
Company runs on AWS; managed services are preferred where they meet the requirements.

acceptableArchitectures.name: Router plus coded workflows (no open-ended agent)
acceptableArchitectures.summary: A model call classifies each message into an intent; each intent runs a coded workflow (tracking lookup; reschedule; update instructions; credit) with model calls only for understanding the request and writing the reply. Authorization, credit policy, the approval step and idempotency keys are in code. Anything outside the known intents goes to a person.
strengths: Predictable, fast and cheap for the 95% of known intents
Easy to test and audit; each path is fixed
tradeoffs: Classification errors become a failure mode to measure

acceptableArchitectures.name: Constrained single agent with scoped tools
acceptableArchitectures.summary: One agent with four narrow tools (track parcel, reschedule, update instructions, request credit), each executing in the customer's scope. The credit tool enforces policy in code, uses an idempotency key derived from the parcel, and returns a pending state for supervisor approval above 10 dollars. Step cap, token budget, per-call timeouts, bounded retries only for safe calls, tracing per conversation, and an escalation path.
strengths: Handles mixed or unusual requests in one conversation
One place to add new tools
tradeoffs: More model calls per conversation: higher cost and latency than a workflow

acceptableArchitectures.name: Managed agent on Bedrock (Bedrock Agents or AgentCore)
acceptableArchitectures.summary: Bedrock Agents with action groups backed by Lambda (least-privilege IAM role per function), or return of control so the application gates credits; or agent code hosted on AgentCore Runtime with Gateway for tools and Observability for traces. Policy, supervisor approval above 10 dollars and idempotency are still enforced in the application or billing integration. Bedrock's user-confirmation feature asks the end user (here the customer) to confirm an action, so it is not the supervisor approval and does not stop a customer who wrote the injected note. All AWS feature details are UNVERIFIED and must be checked.
tradeoffs: Less control over the loop and prompts with the fully managed option
Service limits and features must be verified
The same guardrails are still the team's job
